stories.summary: This article explains the Amiga computer's unique approach to graphics displays, where "screens" are flexible, independently-configured display areas that can have different resolutions and color depths—a capability that set the Amiga apart from modern computers with fixed displays. It covers how Amiga screens use indexed color palettes and planar graphics (bitplanes) to efficiently manage memory and enable multitasking by allowing different programs to run simultaneously on screens with different color requirements. The article focuses on the original OCS hardware, explaining technical specifications like low-res (320x256) and high-res (640x256) modes, special color modes like HAM and EHB, and hardware features that made screen manipulation fast and memory-efficient.

I want to use computer vision to identify visible issues such as dents, scratches, cracked lights, and damaged body panels. The main challenge is that inspection photos can have different lighting conditions, camera angles, image quality, and backgrounds. I am considering an object-detection or image-classification approach, but I am unsure which method would be more appropriate for detecting different types of vehicle damage. What computer-vision approach would you recommend for this type of inspection system? Should I train a custom object-detection model using labeled vehicle-damage images, or would image classification combined with segmentation be more suitable? I am particularly interested in recommendations for preparing the training dataset, handling different lighting and angles, and evaluating the model's accuracy.
